title: Catch drift before the incident
scenario: "Last month someone deleted a private DNS link by hand and the API lost its database for an hour. We only noticed when customers called." — Platform manager
mission: Add scheduled drift detection to CI and prove the foundation layer has no drift today.
objectives: Explain drift as state vs reality
Design a scheduled, read-only workflow with OIDC

prerequisites.notes: Repository variables from session C003 in place.

steps.title: Run a plan locally
steps.detail: Confirm today's baseline: no changes on 10-foundation.

steps.title: Design the workflow
steps.detail: A scheduled workflow (cron) that runs plan for 10-foundation with -detailed-exitcode and fails (or opens an issue) on exit code 2.

steps.title: Mind the identity
steps.detail: Which federated subject will a scheduled run on main present? Make sure it matches an existing credential.

steps.title: Ship it
steps.detail: Branch, PR, required checks green, merge. Trigger it once with workflow_dispatch.

criteria.text: A workflow under .github/workflows has a schedule trigger and runs terraform plan with -detailed-exitcode
The workflow uses OIDC (id-token: write) and no secrets
The latest run of the drift workflow on main succeeded
terraform plan on 10-foundation reports no changes

expectedResult: Drift becomes a red workflow and a notification, not a customer call.

concepts.title: Drift
concepts.body: *Drift* is the difference between what the state/code says and what really exists, usually caused by manual changes. `terraform plan` always refreshes from Azure first, so it shows drift as unexpected changes (for example `+ create` for something that "already existed").

concepts.title: Exit codes make plans automatable
concepts.body: With `-detailed-exitcode`, `terraform plan` exits with 0 (no changes), 1 (error) or 2 (changes present). A pipeline can treat 2 as "drift detected" and alert, without applying anything.

concepts.title: Scheduled workflows
concepts.body: A GitHub workflow with `on: schedule` runs on a cron expression, always on the default branch. Its OIDC subject is therefore `ref:refs/heads/main`. It needs `permissions: id-token: write` to request the OIDC token.

example.title: a nightly job that only reports
example.body: This skeleton runs every night and fails the job on drift (exit code 2). It deliberately never applies:
example.code:
on:
  schedule: [ { cron: "0 6 * * *" } ]
permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "login, init, then: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode"

glossary.def: Terraform reads the real resources before planning.
Schedule syntax: minute hour day month weekday (UTC on GitHub).
Applying automatically to undo drift — risky, it can revert a legitimate emergency change.

recovery: Exit code 1 means the plan itself failed (auth, state lock); 2 means drift. Treat them differently in the workflow.
dont: Do not run apply from the scheduled workflow
Do not use a client secret for the schedule
hints: terraform plan has an option that makes the exit code tell you whether there are changes.
Exit codes: 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes present.
A schedule always runs on the default branch, so its subject is ref:refs/heads/main.

interview.question: How do you detect configuration drift in a Terraform-managed platform?
followUps: What else besides scheduled plans? (locks, policy, activity log alerts)

debrief: Scheduled plan with -detailed-exitcode turns drift into a signal. Auto-apply is risky (it can revert a legitimate emergency change), so most teams alert and require a human PR. Complement with resource locks on critical shared resources (private DNS zones) and activity-log alerts on deletions.

checker.plan: Offline: parse workflow YAML for schedule + -detailed-exitcode + id-token: write. Live: gh run list for the workflow on main; terraform plan -detailed-exitcode on 10-foundation (read-only).
